clinicalPearls: The acute end of the pityriasis lichenoides spectrum, presenting with recurrent crops of erythematous papules that rapidly develop central vesiculation, necrosis, haemorrhagic crust and varioliform (pox-like) scarring.
Lesions at multiple stages of evolution are present simultaneously (a polymorphic picture), typically on the trunk and flexural aspects of the proximal limbs.
More common in children and young adults; individual lesions resolve over weeks but successive crops make the overall course wax and wane over months.
Often follows an infective or immunological trigger, but the pustulo-necrotic lesions themselves are sterile and the condition is not contagious.
Considered a benign clonal T-cell dyscrasia in many cases, sitting on a spectrum with the chronic form (PLC) and, rarely, with lymphomatoid papulosis.
Febrile ulceronecrotic Mucha-Habermann disease is a rare, aggressive variant with high fever, large coalescing necrotic ulcers and systemic upset that can be life-threatening.
Histology shows a wedge-shaped lymphocytic infiltrate, interface change with keratinocyte necrosis, extravasated red cells and lymphocyte exocytosis.
First-line management includes emollients and topical corticosteroids, with oral erythromycin (used for its anti-inflammatory effect) and phototherapy for persistent disease.
reference.pathophysiology: Pityriasis lichenoides et varioliformis acuta is thought to arise from an aberrant, exaggerated host immune response, most often to an antigenic trigger such as a viral or bacterial infection, resulting in a cytotoxic T-cell-driven lymphocytic vasculitis and interface dermatitis. In many patients the infiltrating lymphocytes, predominantly CD8-positive cytotoxic T cells, are monoclonal, supporting the concept of a benign clonal T-cell dyscrasia rather than a simple reactive hypersensitivity; this clonality also underlies the rare biological relationship with lymphomatoid papulosis and cutaneous lymphoma. The cytotoxic attack on keratinocytes and small dermal vessels produces the characteristic wedge-shaped dermal infiltrate, epidermal necrosis, red-cell extravasation and, in severe cases, vessel wall damage with occlusion that generates the deep necrosis and ulceration seen in the febrile ulceronecrotic variant. Proposed triggers include Toxoplasma, Epstein-Barr virus, other viruses and drugs, but no single agent is consistently identified, and the resulting lesions are sterile.
additionalDifferentials: Pityriasis lichenoides chronica (chronic end of the same spectrum)
Lymphomatoid papulosis and other CD30-positive lymphoproliferative disorders
Arthropod bite reactions and papular urticaria
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing wedge-shaped lymphocytic infiltrate, interface change and keratinocyte necrosis
T-cell receptor gene rearrangement studies where a clonal or lymphomatoid process is suspected
Immunohistochemistry including CD30 to distinguish from lymphomatoid papulosis
Investigations for a triggering infection (for example streptococcal, Epstein-Barr virus or Toxoplasma serology) where clinically indicated
Full blood count and inflammatory markers, particularly if systemic symptoms suggest the febrile ulceronecrotic variant
Swabs of ulcerated or crusted lesions to exclude secondary bacterial infection
redFlags: High fever with large, rapidly coalescing necrotic ulcers indicating febrile ulceronecrotic Mucha-Habermann disease
Systemic features such as marked malaise, mucosal involvement or organ dysfunction
Development of persistent nodules or plaques raising concern for lymphomatoid papulosis or lymphoma
Extensive ulceration with signs of secondary sepsis
reference.prognosis: Most cases are self-limiting, resolving over months to a couple of years with only postinflammatory pigment change or varioliform scars, though relapses are common. The rare febrile ulceronecrotic variant carries significant morbidity and can be fatal, requiring urgent systemic treatment.
pitfalls: Mistaking the polymorphic, sterile eruption for chickenpox or another contagious viral illness
Failing to recognise and urgently treat the febrile ulceronecrotic variant
Overlooking clonality or CD30 positivity that signals a lymphoproliferative overlap requiring follow-up
Reassuring patients that scarring will not occur when varioliform scars are common
Assuming a single course of treatment cures it, given the relapsing natural history
management: Emollients and topical corticosteroids for symptomatic relief of localised disease
Oral macrolide or tetracycline antibiotics as first-line systemic anti-inflammatory therapy
Narrowband ultraviolet B phototherapy for widespread or persistent eruptions
Methotrexate for refractory or severe disease

Aggressive treatment of the febrile ulceronecrotic Mucha-Habermann variant with systemic immunosuppression such as methotrexate, systemic corticosteroids or ciclosporin, alongside wound care and fluid and nutritional support
Swabs and antibiotics for secondary bacterial infection of ulcerated lesions
Long-term follow-up with repeat biopsy of atypical lesions to exclude lymphomatoid papulosis or cutaneous lymphoma
Urgent inpatient escalation if high fever, extensive necrosis or systemic upset develop
